slides.title: What Problem Does Async Solve?
slides.content: Synchronous code blocks the calling thread while it waits. During I/O such as a web request or a file read, that means a frozen UI or a server thread that could be doing other work. async/await lets you wait without blocking the thread.
slides.example:
// synchronous: blocks until the download finishes
string s = client.DownloadString(url);
slides.exampleOutput: (blocks here; returns only when the download is complete)

exercise.prompt: An async method is most useful when:
options: It waits on I/O such as a web or file request
It needs to run on a background thread
exercise.answer: It waits on I/O such as a web or file request

slides.title: Tasks Represent Asynchronous Work
slides.content: A Task represents work that is running or will run and completes later. Task<T> is a Task that will eventually produce a value of type T. Awaiting it gives you that T.
slides.exampleOutput: (a Task that will eventually yield an int)

exercise.prompt: What do you get when you await a Task<T>?

slides.title: async and await
slides.content: The async modifier marks a method as asynchronous and lets you use await inside it. The await operator pauses the method at that point until the Task completes, then resumes where it left off.

exercise.prompt: The keyword that pauses an async method until a Task finishes is ______.

slides.title: Awaiting Returns the Result
slides.content: await unwraps the Task: for a Task<T>, the await expression evaluates to T. You can then use the value directly.

exercise.prompt: Complete the line to await the call and receive its value.

slides.title: Async Main
slides.content: By default Main returns void or int. Since C# 7.1, static async Task Main (or Task<int>) is allowed so you can await at the top level of a console program.
slides.exampleOutput: (compiles and runs with awaits permitted in Main)

slides.title: Avoiding Deadlocks
slides.content: .Result and .Wait() block the calling thread and can deadlock (especially under a SynchronizationContext such as a UI thread). Prefer await, and use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code to avoid capturing the context.

exercise.prompt: Which call should you avoid to prevent deadlocks?

slides.title: Error Handling with Await
slides.content: Exceptions thrown by the awaited operation are rethrown where await happens, so wrap await calls in try/catch just like ordinary code.
slides.exampleOutput: (prints the error message if the await throws)

slides.title: Awaiting Multiple Operations
slides.content: To run awaits concurrently and wait for all of them, start each Task without awaiting it, then await Task.WhenAll. This resumes once every one has finished.
slides.exampleOutput: (both start together, resume when both finish)
